rationale: No evidence in the pack mentions any built-in AI image generation tools or design-related AI features in Fedora Workstation; all evidence covers desktop environment, virtualization, containers, and package management topics.
No evidence in the pack mentions password strength checking, breach/compromise detection, or automated password remediation features in Fedora Workstation.
No evidence in the pack mentions browser tab management, grouping, or any browser-level automation feature; the evidence covers OS-level desktop features unrelated to this story.

Fedora Workstation docs claim built-in container tooling with 'no setup required' and easy access to packages/runtimes, suggesting some developer tools are pre-integrated, but this falls short of a full built-in dev suite and requires a single command to fetch tools rather than being pre-installed. No community evidence directly addresses this specific claim.

The evidence pack contains no mention of Raspberry Pi, single-board computers, ARM support, or any certified/optimized SBC experience for Fedora Workstation; all evidence covers desktop apps, DE preferences, and general OS behavior.

Community evidence confirms the existence of official KDE Spins alongside the GNOME-based Workstation default (e.g., 'Fedora 40 KDE Spin', 'Fedora 39 KDE Spin'), showing power-users can choose among desktop environments, but the evidence pack lacks official docs enumerating all variants or their distinct default settings, and includes mixed reports on quality/stability of non-default spins.

Vendor docs explicitly claim container tools work with 'no setup required' and access to Red Hat's registry, directly matching the story, but this is uncorroborated by any hands-on community evidence specifically about container tooling.

No evidence in the pack mentions phone integration, KDE Connect/GSConnect, or clipboard/copy-paste sharing between desktop and phone; the evidence only covers app installation, desktop environments, Wayland, and general Fedora experiences.

The evidence pack covers Fedora Workstation's desktop, containers, GNOME/KDE experience, and Flatpak debates, but contains no mention of running Fedora's terminal environment inside another OS (e.g., WSL) for cross-platform development.

No evidence pack item addresses creating or applying custom system themes; docs mention only dark mode toggling, and community comments discuss GNOME/KDE preferences and Libadwaita design gripes but not custom theming tools or workflows for designers.

Fedora Workstation docs only mention a dark-mode toggle as a visual style option, with no mention of transparency or tint customization; community comments note that GNOME/libadwaita (the default desktop) is limited in style flexibility without extensions, while KDE (a separate spin, not the default Workstation) is described as highly configurable.
Official Fedora Workstation docs explicitly state users can flip a switch for dark mode and use night light to reduce screen glare, directly matching the story's requirements.

Fedora's own docs directly claim a single-command install of all needed packages, tools, and runtimes, plus ready-to-use container tooling, but this is vendor marketing language with no independent community evidence in the pack confirming or detailing an actual single-command dev environment setup (e.g., toolbox, dnf groupinstall).

The evidence pack only contains marketing copy about desktop features (apps, dark mode, VMs, containers) and community discussion of desktop environment preferences; there is no mention of dedicated developer documentation or resources for building software on Fedora Workstation.
No evidence in the pack addresses installation, partitioning, or dual-boot setup alongside another OS; all items concern desktop features, apps, or DE preferences.

No evidence in the pack addresses enterprise-grade security or cross-machine management tooling (e.g., centralized policy management, fleet management, enterprise device management); the evidence only covers desktop UX, package management, containers, and community opinions on DE preferences.

Fedora Workstation provides an app store integrating Fedora repos and Flathub for browsers, chat clients, etc. (fedora-docs-1), and users report solid out-of-box experience (fedora-comm-6, fedora-comm-10). However, community feedback notes friction with Flatpak setup for apps like Discord/Spotify (fedora-comm-14) and gaps for professional/proprietary software like Adobe or CUDA (fedora-comm-8), indicating everyday app coverage isn't fully seamless for all switchers.

The evidence pack contains no mention of installing Fedora Workstation on older/legacy hardware, minimum system requirements, or performance optimizations for aging machines; comments touch on general hardware compatibility (Wi-Fi, Nvidia, laptops) but not low-spec/old hardware support.

Fedora's own docs explicitly describe pressing the Super key and typing to search, matching the exact user story of instant keyboard-shortcut search for apps/files/settings via GNOME Activities Overview.

Fedora's docs directly claim up-to-date packages, runtimes, and container tools available via a single command (fedora-docs-6, fedora-docs-7, fedora-docs-8), aligning with the story. However, community evidence mostly discusses desktop environment quality and Wayland stability rather than confirming toolchain/application freshness, leaving the claim largely vendor-sourced without strong independent validation.

Fedora Workstation ships GNOME Boxes, a built-in tool that lets developers select an OS and create/manage VMs with minimal setup, as documented on the official site; no community evidence contradicts this specific feature.

Fedora's official docs explicitly claim easy install/update/manage of software packages and single-command tool access (fedora-docs-7, fedora-docs-8), but there is no independent/community evidence in the pack validating package manager (dnf) usability, and some community comments raise friction with Flatpak-based software installation (fedora-comm-14, fedora-comm-12), suggesting mixed real-world experience.

No evidence pack items mention password managers, a keyring/vault tool, or private browsing features; the pack only covers app installation, desktop UI, VMs, containers, and general community desktop experience impressions.

One community comment explicitly notes lack of CUDA support, undercutting the AI/ML use case.

The evidence pack contains no mention of the Fedora installer, dual-boot support, partitioning, or replacing/alongside installation of another OS—only unrelated desktop features and community opinions about desktop environments.

No evidence pack item mentions any switcher-specific migration guide or onboarding path from another OS; the docs items describe general feature marketing, not a dedicated transition guide, and community items are general experience anecdotes.
